query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, the absence of cobalt reduces solute pinning—diminishing the formation of stable Cottrell atmospheres—and thereby shifts the dominant dynamic deformation mechanism from dynamic strain aging at low-to-moderate strain rates to phonon‐drag‐controlled dislocation motion at lower thresholds. This altered balance leads to an earlier and more pronounced rate‐dependent increase in yield strength and serrated flow compared to its Co-containing counterpart.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, homogenized solid-solution Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy with a random FCC atomic distribution.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to controlled dynamic deformation tests (e.g., via split-Hopkinson pressure bar or high-speed tensile/compression setups) over a strain rate range from ~1×10⁻³ s⁻¹ to ~1×10³ s⁻¹ at selected temperatures.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under isothermal conditions within a temperature domain where neither dynamic recrystallization nor phase transformations occur (e.g., room temperature up to ~600 °C), ensuring that dislocation-level mechanisms can be isolated.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and mobility of dislocations, the transient (or absent) formation of solute atmospheres, and the extent of phonon-dislocation interactions.
generation.mechanism: Without Co, the alloy’s solute field is weakened so that dislocations are less impeded by solute pinning (i.e. reduced dynamic strain aging). Thus, once deformation is applied at high strain rates, there is insufficient time for re-establishing solute atmospheres and thermal activation to assist dislocation motion. Instead, phonon drag becomes the prevailing resistance, causing a marked, rate-dependent increase in flow stress accompanied by enlarged serration amplitudes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the conventional CoCrFeMnNi alloy, the Co-free variant should (a) exhibit a lower critical strain rate for the transition to a phonon-drag-dominated regime, (b) show a sharper increase in yield strength with increasing strain rate, and (c) display more pronounced serrated flow in its stress–strain curves. Microstructural analyses immediately post-deformation should reveal fewer or less stable solute atmospheres around dislocations.
generation.baseline: Performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested under equivalent strain rate and temperature conditions, in which solute pinning from Co promotes dynamic strain aging over a broader strain-rate range.
generation.boundary: This explanation applies for deformation regimes where the specimen remains a single-phase FCC solid solution (i.e., below temperatures where dynamic recrystallization, martensitic transformations, or twinning-dominated mechanisms become significant) and for strain rates not so extreme as to invoke additional mechanisms (e.g., amorphization under extreme loading).
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extrapolates evidence on phonon drag (PMC7512474::web::013) and solute-dislocation interactions (PMC4655315::web::009) from Co-containing HEAs to the Co-free system; however, direct observations in FeNiCrMn are lacking. There is also uncertainty in the precise strain-rate threshold at which the mechanism shift occurs and whether any compensating effects from other alloying elements may interfere.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and one set of the baseline Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy. Under identical, isothermal dynamic loading (across a broad strain-rate range from ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ to ~10³ s⁻¹ and at a controlled temperature where no phase transformations occur), record full stress–strain responses and perform in-situ or post-mortem microstructural examinations (via high-resolution TEM or analogous methods) focusing on dislocation structures and evidence of solute atmospheres.
measurements: Yield strength and flow stress as functions of strain rate
Amplitude and frequency of serrated flow events in stress–strain curves
Dislocation configurations including the presence or absence of solute atmospheres around dislocations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy does not demonstrate an earlier, significantly enhanced rate-dependent yield strength increase or serration amplitude compared to the Co-containing alloy—in other words, if both alloys show similar dynamic responses and dislocation pinning features—then the hypothesis that the absence of Co shifts the mechanism towards phonon drag dominance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: For HEAs, the model assumes that weak spots are weakened even further upon slipping to model how dislocations break free from the surrounding pinning atoms. This assumption is reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier (PLC) effect or dynamic strain aging. The weak spots re-heal to their original strength during the time between avalanches at a material-specific healing rate, Λ. Specifically, after a weak spot has slipped, the local failure stress, τf,l, drops from its initial value, τs,l, to a lower value, τd,l, by an amount given by the weakening parameter, ε (τs,l − τd,l)/τs,l. It remains at this weakened value until the slip avalanche is completed. Afterwards, τf,l is increased to its initial value, τs,l, at the temperature-dependent healing rate, Λ, until the weak spot slips again during a new avalanche, and the process repeats. The re-strengthening of the weak spots models the rearrangement of atoms around arrested dislocations, leading to the (re-)“pinning” or anchoring of stationary dislocations in place. cited_evidence.text: The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had positive activation volume at strain rates less than 1 × 10−2 s−1. However, when the specimen deformed under high strain rates (beyond 1 × 103 s−1), the deformation time was very short. There was not enough time available for thermal energy to help dislocations overcome the barriers. The NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy had a different deformation mechanism at dynamic loading. According to the literature [], the large jump in yield strength at high strain rates is probably due to the phonon drag effect on the motion of dislocations. The phonon drag phenomenon becomes very effective during plastic deformation at high strain rates []. A phonon is an elastic lattice vibration propagating in a crystal []. The viscous drag generating from the interaction of the dislocations has negative impacts on the deformation progress. The drag effects by the phonons can be ignored under quasi-static conditions for low dislocation velocities. However, high dislocation velocities under high strain rates would enhance the phonon drag effects greatly and lead to phonons scattering, which also hinders dislocation movement.
